description: Ambaji, in Gujarat's Banaskantha district, sits in the Arasur hills of the Aravalli range close to the Rajasthan border. The shrine honours the goddess Shakti as Arasuri Amba and, according to tradition, is one of the Shakta pithas, associated with the heart of Sati. Wikipedia notes that the sanctum has no sculpted image; the goddess is represented by a veiled yantra that devotees do not see directly, and photography inside the sanctum is prohibited. The complex is built of white marble with a gold-plated spire. The temple's own website describes a public trust set up in 1960, chaired by the Banaskantha District Collector. Crowds peak at Navratri and at the Bhadarvi Purnima fair each September.

Official home page: shows a darshan/aarti schedule table for a single date with ambiguous grouping (see notes).

Wikipedia (CC BY-SA): location in Arasur hills, Aravalli range; Shakta pitha tradition; veiled yantra instead of idol; no photography in sanctum; white marble, gold-plated spire; Navratri and Bhadarvi Purnima fair.

Timings NOT used: home page shows two unlabelled groups of aarti/darshan slots for 31 Oct 2026 (07:30-08:00 aarti, 08:00-11:30 and 12:30-16:30 darshan; and 07:00-07:30 aarti, 07:30-09:00 darshan), so which applies when is unclear, and they vary by day/season. Wikipedia says tradition places Sati's heart (one passage says heart or right arm); kept to the official site's 'heart' wording with attribution. No portal listing problem seen (Ambaji is in Banaskantha, Gujarat).

description: The Dwarkadhish Temple, also called Jagat Mandir, stands in Dwarka on Gujarat's western coast and is dedicated to Krishna as the Lord of Dwarka. Wikipedia describes a five-storeyed limestone and sandstone structure facing west, entered through the Swarga Dwar and exited by the Moksha Dwar, with 56 steps leading down to the Gomti ghats. Dwarka is counted among the Char Dham pilgrimage sites, a scheme Wikipedia attributes to Adi Shankara in the Advaita tradition. The temple's own website says the Jagat Mandir complex includes 19 temples, that the Archaeological Survey of India took over the main temple in 1963, and that the Government of Gujarat is sole trustee, with the District Collector as president of its committee. Janmashtami is the chief festival.

description: Trimbakeshwar is a Shiva temple in the town of Trimbak, about 28 km from Nashik in Maharashtra, at the foot of Brahmagiri hill from which the Godavari is described as flowing. It is counted among the twelve Jyotirlingas. According to Wikipedia, the main linga has three faces representing Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva, and the Kushavarta kund within the premises is regarded as a source of the Godavari. The trust's website says the present temple was built by the Peshwa Balaji Bajirao, who ruled 1740-1760, on the site of an older temple; Wikipedia gives two differing attributions for the builder. The Shri Trimbakeshwar Devasthan Trust runs the temple and offers online booking for donation darshan, pujas and pilgrim lodging.

Wikipedia's Kushavarta statement is about the sacred pond; the official site only says the Godavari flows from near Brahmagiri. Portal listing (Nashik, Maharashtra) looks correct.

description: Kumbhariya, in Banaskantha district of northern Gujarat, holds a group of five Svetambara Jain temples carved in marble. According to Wikipedia, they were raised between 1062 and 1231 CE under the Chaulukya rulers, and dedicated to Mahavira, Shantinatha, Parshvanatha, Neminatha and Sambhavanatha; many other temples once stood here but are lost. The complex is cited as a fine example of the Maru-Gurjara style. Features noted include a ceiling in the Mahavira shrine showing scenes from Bahubali's life, a Samavasarana in its porch, and an Ashtapad image in the Shantinatha shrine. Each temple sits in a walled courtyard with a porched gateway. Wikipedia names the Anandji Kalyanji Trust as the managing body, and Mahavir Jayanti as the main festival.

description: The Gop Temple stands at Zinavari (also called Juna or Nana Gop) in Jamjodhpur taluka of Jamnagar district, on the Vartu river below Gop hill in the Barda Hills. Locally known as the Surya Mandir, it is generally dated by Wikipedia to the late sixth century, though scholars have proposed anything from the fifth to the early seventh century. Only the square sanctum survives, about 23 feet high and built of dry-laid stone without mortar, with a hollow, corbelled pyramidal spire crowned by an amalaka and decorated with arched window motifs. Its style is described as an unusual variant of Nagara architecture. The Archaeological Survey of India protects it as a Monument of National Importance.

sources.what_it_supports: Location, Surya dedication, dating debate, architecture, dry-laid construction, ASI protection (N-GJ-133).

Wikipedia notes the shrine's iconography includes Vishnu, Skanda and Shaivite imagery, and radiocarbon dating of a wooden beam is claimed (about 550 CE); I omitted the radiocarbon claim as I could not check its source. Do not confuse with Gop (Odisha) Konark-style temple or Gopnath Mahadev temple. Portal listing (Jamnagar, Gujarat) looks correct; reviewer may add ASI circle page if desired.

description: The Ambika Mata Temple is at Jagat village, roughly 50 km southeast of Udaipur in Rajasthan, set in a cleft of rock. Its presiding deity is Ambika Devi, worshipped as a form of Durga and Shakti. Wikipedia describes it as an early, transitional example of Maru-Gurjara architecture, with a pentagonal layout inside a rampart wall, a pagoda-like gabled roof and small spires around the main tower. Outer walls carry carved celestial musicians, dancers and goddesses, and the article calls it the Khajuraho of Mewar. It says the temple is tied to Rawal Allata of Mewar and that its earliest inscription, of 961 CE, records a repair. Wikipedia says the Rajasthan Department of Archaeology and Museums preserves it.

description: Mangi-Tungi is a Digambar Jain pilgrimage site in the hills of Satana taluka, Nashik district, Maharashtra, with two peaks, Mangi to the west and Tungi to the east. According to Wikipedia, it is regarded as a Siddha Kshetra, and Jain texts link figures such as Rama and Hanuman with liberation here. The hills have old temples and caves, including a Parshvanath cave on Mangi and caves of Chandraprabhu and Rama on Tungi, and the climb to the summit takes roughly 3,500 steps. At the foothill are Jain temples and a Sahastrakoot temple with 1,008 idols. A 108-foot Rishabhanatha figure was consecrated in 2016, and the site's own pages describe a trust office, dharamshala and donation desk.

description: Bhandasar Jain Temple stands in the Bada Bazaar of Bikaner's old walled city, Rajasthan. It is a Svetambara Jain temple dedicated to Sumatinatha, the fifth tirthankara, and is credited to Bhanda Shah, an Oswal merchant, after whom it is named. Its date is debated: Wikipedia and the Archaeological Survey of India inventory give the 12th century, while a Jio Institute exhibit cites inscriptional and stylistic evidence for the 15th to 16th century. The three-storey sandstone shrine has a white spire over a red pancharatha sanctum and a domed hall. It is best known for painted walls and ceilings, with Krishna scenes outside and Jain narratives and gold-embossed work within. Local legend says ghee was used in the mortar. The ASI has nominal jurisdiction, and a local Jain trust cares for it.

description: Lodurva, also spelled Lodhruva, is a village in Jaisalmer district, Rajasthan, whose Jain temple is the one surviving structure of an older ruined town. According to Wikipedia, the Bhati ruler Deoraj made Lodhruva his capital in the 8th to 9th century, and the temple is said to date from that time; it was reportedly plundered, then repaired in 1615 and largely rebuilt in the late 1970s, with more restoration since. It is a Svetambara temple whose main image is Parshvanatha in black marble under a thousand-hooded canopy, with a shrine to Sambhavanatha in the complex. Built of yellow Jaisalmer stone, it is noted for its ornate gateway arch, lattice screens and kalpavriksha carvings. Wikipedia names the Sri Jaisalmer Lodravpur Parshwanath Jain Shwetamber Trust as its manager.

description: Osian is a town in Jodhpur district, Rajasthan, about 69 km north of Jodhpur, with a cluster of Hindu and Jain temples that Wikipedia dates to the 8th to 12th century. Two stand out for pilgrims. The Mahavira Jain temple is a Svetambara tirtha of the Oswal Jain community; according to tradition and Wikipedia it was founded under the Pratihara king Vatsaraja, though its dates are debated, and it has an ornate gateway arch, side shrines and a large Mahavira image. The Archaeological Survey of India protects it, and Wikipedia names Seth Shri Mangalsinghji Ratansinghji Dev ki Pedhi as its governing body. Sachiya Mata temple sits on a hill to its northeast. Jain tradition holds that Acharya Ratnaprabhasuri made the goddess, earlier Chamunda, a protector of the temple and the Oswal clan.

description: Ramdevra is a village about 12 km north of Pokhran in Jaisalmer district, Rajasthan, and the seat of the Baba Ramdev temple, also called Ramdeora. The shrine honours Baba Ramdevji, a Tanwar Rajput folk saint whom devotees revere across caste and religion. Wikipedia gives conflicting dates for his samadhi, 1384 and 1459, and says Maharaja Ganga Singh of Bikaner built a temple around it in 1931. The Incredible India page describes the sanctum as holding a seated image of the saint with a camel beside him, and says pilgrims, many arriving on foot, are offered free meals and shelter. A large fair, the Ramdevra Mela, runs from Bhadrapada Shukla 2 to 10, roughly August to September, drawing devotees from several states. Wikipedia does not name a managing trust.

description: Shri Mahaveer Ji is a Jain pilgrimage town in the Hindaun block of Karauli district, Rajasthan, beside the Gambhir River. The principal shrine is dedicated to Mahavira, shown seated in padmasana in a sandstone image of modest size, and the site belongs to the Digambara tradition. According to Wikipedia, the temple was raised in the 17th century by a merchant, Amar Chand Bilala, after the image was unearthed; the legend tells of a farmer whose cow released milk over a mound where the idol was later found. The complex includes a tall marble column at the gate, the Shantinath Jinalaya and a mirror-work temple. A five-day fair around Mahavir Jayanti ends with a bullock-cart procession. Wikipedia says the Shri Mahaveer Ji Trust governs it.

description: Shree Siddhivinayak is a Ganesha temple in Prabhadevi, Mumbai, where the deity is worshipped as Siddhivinayak, the Ganesha who grants wishes. The trust's own page says the shrine was first consecrated on 19 November 1801 and began as a small structure holding a black stone idol. It describes the image as roughly two and a half feet wide with the trunk turned to the right, four hands, and Riddhi and Siddhi standing on either side, with an eye marked on the forehead. According to Wikipedia, the wooden sanctum doors are carved with the Ashtavinayaka and the inner roof is gold plated. It is managed by the Shree Siddhivinayak Ganapati Temple Trust, which runs donation, pooja booking, medical help and a book bank.

description: Shri Mahalakshmi Temple stands on Bhulabhai Desai Road at Mahalaxmi, on the sea side of south Mumbai. Its sanctum holds three goddesses of the Tridevi: Mahalakshmi, Mahakali and Mahasaraswati. According to Wikipedia, the merchant Dhakji Dadaji built it, completing the work in 1831, and the site also recounts a legend linking the shrine to the Hornby Vellard sea-reclamation project. The Mahalakshmi image is regarded by devotees as living, and visitor numbers rise sharply during Navaratri and Diwali, with Lakshmi Puja and Gudi Padwa among the notable occasions. The temple is run by the Shri Mahalaxmi Temple Trust.

description: Shrimant Dagdusheth Halwai Ganpati Temple is in Budhvar Peth, in the old centre of Pune, and is dedicated to Ganesha. According to the trust, the shrine began with the sweet-maker Dagdusheth Halwai and his wife Lakshmibai after they lost their only son to plague. Wikipedia adds that the present image is the third installed by the family, set within a simple structure that allows the idol to be seen from outside, with two marble guardians at the entrance. The trust's site links the temple to the growth of Pune's public Ganpati festival, and it is a focal point during the ten-day Ganeshotsav. The Shreemant Dagdusheth Halwai Sarvajanik Ganpati Trust manages it and also supports education, an old age home and microfinance work.

It stands within a temple complex that also includes Dwarkamai, Gurusthan and Chavadi, each part of the daily worship round. The programme published by the trust includes a morning aarti, an afternoon Pothi reading, evening devotional songs and a closing Shej Aarti at 10 PM. Shri Sai Baba Sansthan Trust, Shirdi describes itself as the governing and administrative body of the Samadhi temple and the other temples on the premises, and also runs a hospital, a blood bank, colleges and a free meal service for visitors.

description: Babulnath is a Shiva temple on a small hill beside Chowpatty and Malabar Hill in south Mumbai, where the deity is worshipped as Babulnath. Its site gives several explanations of the name, the best known crediting a cowherd called Babul who is said to have found a self-manifested Shivling there. The trust's account says a present-day temple grew from a small shrine and was enlarged between 1836 and 1840 with public donations, with shrines to other deities added later. It records a court judgment of 1808 in the temple's favour in a dispute with neighbouring Parsis, and a 1883 ruling placing the temple in public charity under trustees. The site names the organisation as Shree Babulnath Mandir Charities.

description: The Dilwara temples stand in a forested hill range about 2.5 km from Mount Abu in Sirohi district, Rajasthan, and belong to the Svetambara Jain tradition. According to Wikipedia, five temples sit inside one walled compound, dedicated to Rishabhanatha, Neminatha, Parshvanatha and Mahavira, and they are counted among the five great tirthas of the Svetambara sect. They are built of white marble in the Solanki (Maru-Gurjara) style and are noted for fine carving, especially in Vimal Vasahi and Luna Vasahi, where the latter has a central dome with rings of tirthankara and monk figures. Wikipedia says the temples are administered from Sirohi by the Seth Kalyanji Parmanandji Pedhi, which also runs a nearby dining hall.

description: The Ranakpur Jain temple is in the village of Ranakpur near Sadri in Pali district, Rajasthan, and is dedicated to Rishabhanatha (Adinatha), the first tirthankara of the Svetambara Jain tradition. According to Wikipedia, it is built mainly of white marble in the Maru-Gurjara style and is known for carved pillars said to number about 1,444, none of them identical, along with numerous domes and a main shrine holding a four-faced image of Adinatha. Tradition credits a merchant named Dharna Shah, with the patronage of Rana Kumbha of Mewar, though sources disagree on the dates. The article says the temple is managed by the Anandji Kalyanji Pedhi, and the campus has a dharmshala and dining hall for pilgrims.

description: Tanot Mata temple lies in Jaisalmer district in western Rajasthan, roughly 122 km from Jaisalmer city and close to the Pakistan border. According to Wikipedia, the goddess is Tanot Mata, identified with Aavad, a daughter of Mamadia Charan and regarded in Charan literature as an incarnation of Hinglaj Mata. A temple priest is quoted as saying that the Bhati king Tanu Rao built the shrine in 828 AD. The temple is best known for local accounts that about 3,000 shells fired toward it in the 1965 war failed to explode or missed; the Border Security Force reportedly took over its management afterwards. A victory tower commemorating the Battle of Longewala stands in the compound.

description: Nakodaji is a Shvetambara Jain pilgrimage site in Barmer district of Rajasthan, located between the villages of Vikrampura and Nakoda near Mewanagar. Its central image is Parshvanatha, a 24-inch black stone idol, and the complex also enshrines Nakoda Bhairava, a guardian deity revered by both Jains and Hindus. According to Wikipedia, Jain legend credits Acharya Sthulabhadra with the original shrine, the present structure dates to the Solanki era, and the main image was reinstalled in 1449 after being hidden from an invader. The marble and sandstone temple has many small domed sub-shrines, a basement chamber of idols, and a guest house and community kitchen. Wikipedia names a Nakoda Parshwanath Tirth Trust as its administrator.

description: Shankheshwar is a town in Patan district of Gujarat, and its Jain temple stands in the middle of the town on the bank of the Rupen river. It is a Shvetambara Jain pilgrimage site dedicated to Parshvanatha, whose main image is a white marble figure about 182 cm tall in the seated lotus posture. Wikipedia reports a tradition tying the site to the ancient settlement Shankhapur and records rebuilding and renovation episodes in the 11th to 13th centuries, with the present temple built in 1811. The complex has an assembly hall, several courtyards and many subsidiary shrines, plus facilities for pilgrims such as a dining hall. Large gatherings occur on the Posh Dashami day and at Diwali. The page does not name the managing body.

description: The Palitana temples crown the Shatrunjaya hills, about 2 km south of Palitana town in Bhavnagar district, Gujarat. They belong to the Shvetambara Murtipujaka tradition of Jainism and form one of its most important pilgrimage sites. Wikipedia describes roughly 900 shrines and larger temples grouped in fortified enclosures called tuks along the ridges, with the principal temple dedicated to Rishabhanatha, the first Tirthankara. Jain tradition links the hill to remote antiquity, though Wikipedia says the surviving temples date from about the 11th century onward. Pilgrims climb roughly 3,500 stone steps from the town, and sources say no one stays overnight on the hill and the temples close in the monsoon. The Anandji Kalyanji Trust is reported to manage them.

description: Morgaon, a village on the Karha river in Baramati taluka of Pune district, is home to the Mayureshwar (Moreshwar) temple, a Ganesha shrine regarded as the starting and ending point of the Ashtavinayak circuit. The trust's site calls the temple Sri Mayureshvara and links it with the saint Morya Gosavi. The walled complex has four minaret-like corner pillars, a large Nandi facing the shrine, a stone mouse figure, an assembly hall and a Nagnabhairava shrine. Wikipedia notes four gates facing the cardinal directions and a self-manifested, sindoor-covered image, and says its construction date is unknown. Festivals include Ganesh Chaturthi and Ganesh Jayanti, and the Chinchwad Deosthan Trust administers the temple.

description: Theur is a village in Haveli taluka of Pune district, near the meeting of the Bhima and Mula-Mutha rivers, and its Chintamani temple is one of the eight Ashtavinayak Ganesha shrines of Maharashtra. According to Wikipedia, the exact age of the present building is unknown; it is attributed to the saint Morya Gosavi or his descendant, and the Peshwa ruler Madhavrao I renovated it and added a wooden assembly hall. The image of Ganesha is considered self-manifested and is coated with sindoor. Wikipedia notes a large bell donated by Chimaji Appa and the Peshwa palace behind the temple. The trust's site mentions Peshwa-era jewellery on the deity and major festivals in Bhadrapada and Magha. The Chinchwad Deosthan Trust runs the temple.
